Based on the search results, here's what I found about arXiv paper 2201.11227:

## Overview

Synchromesh is a framework for substantially improving the reliability of pre-trained models for code generation. The paper was submitted on January 26, 2022 by Gabriel Poesia, Oleksandr Polozov, Vu Le, Ashish Tiwari, Gustavo Soares, Christopher Meek, and Sumit Gulwani.

## Problem

Large pre-trained language models have been used to generate code from natural language specifications, but they often violate syntactic and semantic rules of their output language, limiting their practical usability.

## Solution

Synchromesh comprises two components: it retrieves few-shot examples from a training bank using Target Similarity Tuning (TST), a novel method for semantic example selection, then feeds the examples to a pre-trained language model and samples programs using Constrained Semantic Decoding (CSD), a general framework for constraining the output to a set of valid programs in the target language.

You can access the full paper on arXiv at https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.11227

I found comprehensive information about the paper "Monitor-Guided Decoding of Code LMs with Static Analysis of Repository Context" from NeurIPS 2023.

## Key Information:

**Overview:**
Monitor-guided decoding (MGD) is proposed where a monitor uses static analysis to guide the decoding. The approach addresses the limitation that language models struggle when it becomes necessary to use types, functionality or APIs defined elsewhere in the repository or a linked library, especially those not seen during training, as LMs suffer from limited awareness of such global context and end up hallucinating.

**Approach:**
The work proposes monitors as a stateful interface between LMs and static analysis, where a monitor observes the code generated by an LM and queries static analysis at pre-defined trigger points, with suggestions converted to masks used for reshaping the logits (token-generation probabilities) produced by the LM in subsequent decoding steps.

**Dataset & Evaluation:**
The researchers construct a repository-level dataset PragmaticCode for method-completion in Java and evaluate MGD on it. On models of varying parameter scale, by monitoring for type-consistent object dereferences, MGD consistently improves compilation rates and agreement with ground truth.

**Resources:**
The official code and data artifact is hosted on GitHub as the monitors4codegen repository.

SPIRES (Structured Prompt Interrogation and Recursive Extraction of Semantics) is a method for populating knowledge bases using zero-shot learning, published in Bioinformatics, Volume 40, Issue 3 in March 2024.

SPIRES is a Knowledge Extraction approach that relies on the ability of Large Language Models (LLMs) to perform zero-shot learning and general-purpose query answering from flexible prompts. Given a detailed, user-defined knowledge schema and input text, SPIRES recursively performs prompt interrogation against an LLM to obtain responses matching the provided schema.

Key features of SPIRES include:

- It requires no model tuning or training data
- SPIRES uses existing ontologies and vocabularies to provide identifiers for matched elements
- It has been applied in different domains, including extraction of food recipes, multi-species cellular signaling pathways, disease treatments, multi-step drug mechanisms, and chemical to disease relationships

SPIRES is available as part of the open source OntoGPT package on GitHub.

The article reference (btae104) corresponds to the DOI 10.1093/bioinformatics/btae104, and the lead author is J. Harry Caufield.

**Guiding LLMs The Right Way: Fast, Non-Invasive Constrained Generation** is a paper by Luca Beurer-Kellner, Marc Fischer, and Martin Vechev, published at ICML 2024.

## Overview

The paper addresses constrained decoding methods, which propose to enforce strict formal language constraints during generation to ensure that text generated by LLMs is in an expected format.

## Key Problem

The authors show that existing constrained decoding methods not only incur performance overhead during generation, but many also significantly impair task accuracy if they do not correctly align the underlying LLM sub-word vocabularies with external constraints.

## Solution

The paper presents a novel decoding algorithm called DOMINO that can enforce constraints in a fully subword-aligned fashion, while leveraging pre-computation and speculative decoding to achieve virtually no overhead and in some cases even almost 2× speedup over unconstrained decoding.

The paper was published on February 7, 2024, and is available through multiple sources including the ICML proceedings and arXiv.

The paper "Open Information Extraction with Entity Focused Constraints" was authored by Prajna Upadhyay, Oana Balalau, and Ioana Manolescu. It was published in the Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EACL 2023, pages 1285–1296, in Dubrovnik, Croatia.

The paper addresses Open Information Extraction (OIE), which is the task of extracting tuples of the form (subject, predicate, object), without any knowledge of the type and lexical form of the predicate, the subject, or the object. The authors focus on improving OIE quality by exploiting domain knowledge about the subject and object, specifically exploring how to inject constraints in the extraction through constrained inference and constraint-aware training when subjects and objects are named entities.

Through a carefully constructed training dataset and constrained training, the authors obtained a 29.17% F1-score improvement in the CaRB metric and a 24.37% F1-score improvement in the WIRe57 metric.

The paper is available at the ACL Anthology: https://aclanthology.org/2023.findings-eacl.95/

**"Guided Open Vocabulary Image Captioning with Constrained Beam Search"** by Peter Anderson, Basura Fernando, Mark Johnson, and Stephen Gould was published in the Proceedings of the 2017 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP), pages 936–945, in Copenhagen, Denmark.

**Key contributions:**

The paper presents a flexible approach that enables existing deep captioning architectures to take advantage of image taggers at test time without re-training. The method uses constrained beam search to force the inclusion of selected tag words in the output, and fixed, pretrained word embeddings to facilitate vocabulary expansion to previously unseen tag words.

**Main results:**

The approach achieves state-of-the-art results for out-of-domain captioning on MSCOCO (with improved results for in-domain captioning), and significantly outperforms approaches that incorporate the same tag predictions into the learning algorithm. The method also significantly improves the quality of generated ImageNet captions by leveraging ground-truth labels.

The paper is available on the ACL Anthology (https://aclanthology.org/D17-1098/) and arXiv (https://arxiv.org/abs/1612.00576).

## Paper Information

The paper "DeepStruct: Pretraining of Language Models for Structure Prediction" was published in the Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: ACL 2022 by Chenguang Wang, Xiao Liu, Zui Chen, Haoyun Hong, Jie Tang, and Dawn Song.

## Paper Overview

The paper introduces a method for improving the structural understanding abilities of language models. Unlike previous approaches that finetune models with task-specific augmentation, the authors pretrain language models on a collection of task-agnostic corpora to generate structures from text.

## Key Results

The approach is evaluated on 28 datasets, spanning 10 structure prediction tasks including open information extraction, joint entity and relation extraction, named entity recognition, relation classification, semantic role labeling, event extraction, coreference resolution, factual probe, intent detection, and dialogue state tracking. A 10B parameter language model transfers non-trivially to most tasks and obtains state-of-the-art performance on 21 of 28 datasets that were evaluated.

You can access the paper through the ACL Anthology at the doi reference: 10.18653/v1/2022.findings-acl.67, and the code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/cgraywang/deepstruct.

The paper addresses an important problem in relation extraction. Recent works on relation extraction applying the distant supervision paradigm employ existing knowledge bases as a source of supervision; however, these approaches assume each sentence mentioning two related entities expresses the given relation, which leads to noisy patterns that hurt precision, particularly if the knowledge base is not directly related to the text.

The authors present a novel approach using a factor graph to explicitly model the decision whether two entities are related and whether this relation is mentioned in a given sentence, and apply constraint-driven semi-supervision to train the model without knowledge about which sentences express the relations.

The work addresses the issue that while language models of code work well when surrounding code provides sufficient context, they struggle when it becomes necessary to use types, functionality or APIs defined elsewhere in the repository or a linked library, especially those not seen during training, as LMs suffer from limited awareness of such global context and end up hallucinating.
